    What is the meaning of the word fortune?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    fortune
    /ˈfôrCHən/
    Fortune refers to
    a large amount of wealth or to chance/luck, often influencing a person's fate. It signifies substantial assets (e.g., "made a fortune") or favorable events (e.g., "good fortune"). Synonyms include wealth, riches, prosperity, luck, chance, fate, and destiny. 
    Usage Examples 
    • Wealth: "She inherited a vast fortune from her aunt". "That car costs a small fortune".
    • Luck/Chance: "He had the good fortune to survive the accident". "Their fortunes changed for the better".
    • Destiny: "The reporter tried to tell her fortune using tarot cards". 
    Common Synonyms and Related Terms 
    • Wealth: Assets, riches, capital, treasure, means, bounty, pot.
    • Luck/Chance: Fate, destiny, lot, fluke, serendipity, hazard. 
    Key Nuances 
    • Fortune vs. Misfortune: While "fortune" often implies good luck or wealth, it can refer to either positive or negative events when describing a "fortune".
    • Telling Fortune: The act of predicting someone's future.

      AI Overview
      A one-year Fortune magazine subscription typically costs around $29.98 for 6 print issues, often found through discount sites like MagazineLine or DiscountMags, making it about $5 per issue, though prices vary with deals and renewal offers, with single issues costing more and digital access potentially free with Kindle Unlimited. 
      Typical Pricing & Offers:
      • Discount Sites: Look for $29.98 for 1 year (6 issues), equating to $5 per issue. 
      • Multi-Year: Offers might extend to $59.96 for 2 years or $89.94 for 3 years. 
      • Single Issues: Higher cost, potentially $15.99 plus shipping from some sources. 
      • Newsstand: Can be significantly higher, around $89.91 for a year. 
      • Digital: Free with a Kindle Unlimited membership for some content. 
      Where to Check: 
      • Discount Services: MagazineLine, DiscountMags.com.
      • Official Sources: Fortune's own subscription page.
      • Retailers: Barnes & Noble.
      Key Takeaway: Promotional pricing often brings the cost down to about $5 per issue for a year's subscription, but always compare offers and check for auto-renewal terms.

        businessman Chatchaval Jiaravanon
        The company is headquartered in New York City and is owned by Thai businessman Chatchaval Jiaravanon. The magazine Fortune was the 1930 creation of Henry Luce, co-founder of Time Incorporated, which at its peak was both the largest magazine publisher in the United States and the world.

        History. What is the history of Fortune magazine?
        About this result
        Feedback
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        Fortune magazine was launched by Henry Luce in 1930 as a lavish, intellectual publication exploring American industry, known for its art, deep dives into corporations, and pioneering use of photojournalism, eventually becoming famous for its annual "Fortune 500" list and evolving through different ownerships, competing with Forbes, and adapting to modern media, remaining a leading global business publication.
         
        Founding & Early Years (1930s-1940s)
        • Vision:
          Founded by Time Inc.'s Henry Luce (co-founder of Time), Fortune aimed to be a "de luxe" magazine for business leaders, showcasing industrial life with beautiful Art Deco design, photography (Walker Evans, Margaret Bourke-White), and in-depth articles. 
        • Content:
          It featured long "corporation stories," public opinion polls (pioneered by Elmo Roper), and essays on society, politics, and economics, attracting writers like John Kenneth Galbraith and Daniel Bell. 
        • Success:
          Despite launching during the Great Depression, it thrived by covering business's role in society, establishing itself as an authoritative voice for the elite. 
        Evolution & Modern Era (1950s-Present)
        • Publication Schedule:
          Started monthly, shifted to bi-weekly in 1978, then every three weeks, and now publishes about 14 times a year, according to Fortune. 
        • The Fortune 500:
          Its annual list of America's largest corporations became a benchmark for business success, becoming an enduring legacy. 
        • Ownership Changes:
          Remained part of Time Inc. until Meredith Corporation acquired Time Inc. in 2018, then sold Fortune to Thai businessman Chatchaval Jiaravanon in late 2018. 
        Key Features & Impact
        • Visuals:
          Known for distinctive covers (Art Deco, modernist) and high-quality photography. 
        • Authority:
          Maintains high authority in business, competing with Forbes and Bloomberg Businessweek. 
        • Legacy:
          Continues to provide in-depth analysis, corporate rankings (Fortune 500, Global 500), and cover global business trends through its website, events (Fortune Forum), and print magazine.

          AI Overview
          Fortune magazine targets high-level business professionals, including CEOs, C-suite executives, entrepreneurs, and investors, seeking in-depth analysis on corporate leadership, global economic trends, technology, and management strategies to help them succeed and make informed decisions, with a focus on big companies and influential figures. The audience values insights into business innovation, financial markets, and stories of major corporate players, often including affluent individuals with significant net worth.
           
          Key Audience Characteristics:
          • Senior Executives: CEOs, CFOs, COOs, and other top management. 
          • Business Leaders: Entrepreneurs, investors, and decision-makers in large corporations. 
          • Affluent Individuals: Readers with high net worth and income, interested in luxury and investment. 
          • Professionals Seeking Growth: Those looking for actionable insights on leadership, management, and industry trends. 
          What They Look For:
          • Corporate Insights: Deep dives into major companies, their practices, and the people leading them. 
          • Economic Trends: Analysis of global markets, new technologies, and shifting industries. 
          • Leadership Development: Content that helps them become better managers and leaders. 
          • Influential Lists: The famous Fortune 500 and other rankings that identify top companies and leaders. 
          In essence, Fortune serves the elite business community, providing them with a definitive voice on business that helps them stay ahead in a complex global environment.

            Notable Features. What are the notable features of Fortune magazine?

            Feedback
            An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
            AI Overview
            Fortune magazine's notable features include its iconic rankings (Fortune 500, Global 500, World's Most Admired Companies), in-depth investigative business journalism, high artistic quality with commissioned artwork and photography (like by Walker Evans, Jacob Lawrence), and its focus on "how to be a better manager," distinguishing it with deep analysis rather than just getting rich.
             
            Key Features & Content
            • Iconic Rankings: Famous for its annual lists like the Fortune 500, Fortune Global 500, and World's Most Admired Companies, which are highly influential in business. 
            • In-Depth Reporting: Known for meticulous, long-form articles providing deep analysis of companies, industries, and global economic trends. 
            • Artistic & Literary Quality: From its launch, Fortune was designed to be visually stunning, commissioning original art, commissioning prominent artists like Diego Rivera, and featuring renowned writers such as James Agee and Archibald MacLeish. 
            • Focus on Management: While covering business, its core focus is often on management, strategy, and societal impact, aiming to make readers "better managers". 
            • Broad Scope: Covers a wide range of topics, from corporate stories and economic issues to technology and social dynamics. 
            Historical Significance
            • Pioneering Business Journalism: Revolutionized business media with high production values and literary standards during the Depression, making business accessible and interesting.
            • Social Conscience: Developed a reputation for covering social issues and the interconnectedness of business and government during the New Deal era.
